blocks.orig: Just as diverse as the Tanzanian landscape – we only say mountains, savannahs, jungles, crater, lakes, crater lakes – are the people calling this East African gem their home. The country is inhabited by over 100 ethnic groups, who of course all have their own language. With more than 120 languages and dialects, Tanzania has more than any other African country, creating an unparalleled cultural depth.
blocks.html: The people who live in this East African gem are every bit as varied as its landscape – think mountains, savannahs, jungles, crater, lakes and crater lakes. More than 100 ethnic groups make the country their home, and naturally each has a language of its own. Counting over 120 languages and dialects, Tanzania has more than any other country in Africa, which gives it a cultural depth without equal.

blocks.orig: Even without this information, you might have wondered whether your English will see you through when travelling to Tanzania, right? Spoiler alert: you’ll be fine! Nevertheless, we’ll have a look at the main languages spoken in Tanzania and even provide you with some basic Swahili skills. The more you know…
blocks.html: Even before reading this, you may have asked yourself whether your English will be enough on a trip to Tanzania, haven’t you? Spoiler: it will! Still, let’s look at the main languages spoken in Tanzania, and we will even give you a few basic Swahili skills. The more you know…

blocks.orig: How many languages are there in Tanzania?
blocks.html: How many languages does Tanzania have?

blocks.orig: A total of 126 languages are spoken in Tanzania, with Swahili and English being the two official ones. On top of these, there are approximately 18 developing, 58 vigorous, 40 endangered, and 8 dying languages.
blocks.html: Altogether, 126 languages are spoken in Tanzania, two of which – Swahili and English – are official. Besides these, there are roughly 18 developing, 58 vigorous, 40 endangered and 8 dying languages.

blocks.orig: What is the most spoken language in Tanzania?
blocks.html: Which language is spoken most in Tanzania?

blocks.orig: Spoken by approximately 90% of the Tanzanian population, that would be Swahili. It’s also called Kiswahili by Tanzanians, and it is the primary social, political, and educational language.
blocks.html: That is Swahili, spoken by about 90% of the people of Tanzania. Tanzanians also call it Kiswahili, and it is the main language of social life, politics and education.

blocks.orig: The second institutional language is English. It has, however, been used as a second or third language and is taught in schools. The level isn’t the best, though, so people might be able to read the language but might have a harder time understanding it.
blocks.html: English is the second institutional language. Even so, it has served as a second or third language and is taught in schools. The standard is not very high, however, so people may be able to read English yet find it harder to understand when spoken.

blocks.orig: It’s generally accepted that the language developed as a result of trade between the coast people of East Africa and the Arabs, and that its core originates in Bantu languages. Around the 19th century, many Tanzanians and Kenyans started identifying as Swahili. After the country’s independence, Swahili became Tanzania’s national language to unify the new nation.
blocks.html: The common view is that the language grew out of trade between the Arabs and the coastal peoples of East Africa, with a core rooted in Bantu languages. From around the 19th century, many Kenyans and Tanzanians began to identify as Swahili. Once the country was independent, Swahili was made Tanzania’s national language to bring the new nation together.

blocks.orig: As of today, Swahili is the primary language used in Tanzania and the government keeps advocating it becoming the one and only official Tanzanian language. Swahili has recently become the primary language used throughout the educational system. This decision made Tanzania the first sub-Saharan country to introduce a native African language as the only official language of education.
blocks.html: Swahili is now the main language in Tanzania, and the government continues to push for it to be the sole official Tanzanian language. Recently Swahili also became the main language throughout the education system. With this decision, Tanzania became the first sub-Saharan country to make a native African language the only official language of education.

blocks.orig: English was the dominant language in Tanzania during the British colonial period from 1919 to 1961. After Tanganyika and Zanzibar became the independent United Republic of Tanzania, however, it was dethroned by Swahili.
blocks.html: During the British colonial period, from 1919 to 1961, English was Tanzania’s dominant language. Once Tanganyika and Zanzibar had become the independent United Republic of Tanzania, though, Swahili took its place.

blocks.orig: For a long time, English remained the primary language of secondary and higher education. As just mentioned, this is no longer the case, with Swahili now being the language used across the educational system.
blocks.html: English long stayed the main language of secondary and higher education. As mentioned above, that has changed, and Swahili is now used throughout the education system.

blocks.orig: Still, English remains relatively popular, and you’re sure to encounter numerous English speakers on your Tanzanian adventures, especially in major cities and tourist areas.
blocks.html: Even so, English is still fairly popular, and on your travels in Tanzania you will certainly meet plenty of people who speak it, above all in the larger cities and tourist areas.

blocks.orig: Other widely spoken language in Tanzania
blocks.html: Other languages widely spoken in Tanzania

blocks.orig: Now that we’ve given you an overview of the official languages of Tanzania, it’s time to look at some lesser-known yet still widely spoken languages of Tanzania.
blocks.html: With this overview of the official languages of Tanzania behind us, let’s turn to a few less well-known but still widely spoken languages in Tanzania.

blocks.orig: These are the ethnic languages used in more spread-out communities and peoples. However, while they may not be as widely spoken or even recognized as official languages by the Tanzanian government, these languages are just as important to the cultural landscape as any other.
blocks.html: These are ethnic languages spoken by more scattered communities and peoples. They may be less widely spoken, and the Tanzanian government may not recognise them as official languages, yet they matter to the cultural landscape just as much as any other.

blocks.orig: So, what other native Tanzania languages can you encounter when travelling through this marvellous country?
blocks.html: Which other native Tanzania languages might you come across, then, as you travel through this marvellous country?

blocks.orig: Kisankasa is a good example of how diverse and rich the country’s linguistics is, as it’s a Bantu language that is still in wide use. The language is spoken by about half of the Kisi people who are from the Njombe region.
blocks.html: Kisankasa shows well how rich and varied the country’s linguistics are: it is a Bantu language that is still widely used. Roughly half of the Kisi people, who come from the Njombe region, speak it.

blocks.orig: Pare is also a Bantu language group spoken by the Pare people in the northeast of Tanzania and also known as Chasu, Athu, and Chathu. About 500,000 people communicate in Pare, making it being used more than other dialects and some indigenous languages.
blocks.html: Pare, also called Chasu, Athu and Chathu, is another Bantu language group, spoken by the Pare people in north-east Tanzania. Around 500,000 people use Pare to communicate, so it is used more than other dialects and some indigenous languages.

blocks.orig: Bemba is spoken in the southern part of Tanzania, but also in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. It’s a common or bridge language used by most of the country’s indigenous people and also known as Chibemba, Cibemba, and Ichibemba, just to name a few variations.
blocks.html: Bemba is spoken in southern Tanzania, as well as in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. Most of the country’s indigenous people use it as a common or bridge language, and it goes by names such as Chibemba, Cibemba and Ichibemba, to mention just a few variations.

blocks.orig: Hehe has a complex tense-aspect-mood system that is native to the Iringa region, which you can find south of the great Ruaha River. The language is spoken by fewer than 200,000 people and has lost some of its distinct features over the last 150 years or so.
blocks.html: Hehe, native to the Iringa region, which lies south of the great Ruaha River, has a complex tense-aspect-mood system. Fewer than 200,000 people speak the language, and over roughly the last 150 years it has lost some of its distinctive features.

blocks.orig: Other popular indigenous languages include Maasai, Digo, Datooga, and Chindali. We know Tanzania in and out (the name Your Tanzania Trip didn’t come out of nowhere), and we’re still discovering the dialects and indigenous sub-languages spoken by different tribes. Exploring just never gets boring 😉
blocks.html: Maasai, Digo, Datooga and Chindali are among the other popular indigenous languages. We know Tanzania inside out (the name Your Tanzania Trip did not appear out of thin air), and still we keep discovering the dialects and indigenous sub-languages of different tribes. Exploring simply never gets dull 😉

blocks.orig: It’s natural for languages to slowly fade and eventually die. That’s especially true for countries with diverse linguistic landscapes, like Tanzania.
blocks.html: Languages fading slowly and finally dying out is a natural process, all the more so in countries with a varied linguistic landscape such as Tanzania.

blocks.orig: One of these languages in Tanzania is Asa from the Asa people in the northern region of Tanzania. However, today it isn’t spoken by anyone natively. Some forms of words might still have some meaning to specific communities, but some are distant memory of an older generation.
blocks.html: In Tanzania, one such language is Asa, from the Asa people of the country’s northern region. Nobody speaks it natively any more, though. Certain word forms may still mean something to particular communities, while others are a fading memory of an older generation.

blocks.orig: To be honest: it can be difficult to track each of the approximately 126 native languages in Tanzania. As easy as some are to identify, political decisions play a big role in what languages they want to promote and integrate within their communities.
blocks.html: Honestly, keeping track of all of the roughly 126 native languages in Tanzania is not easy. Some may be simple to identify, but political decisions have a large influence on which languages are promoted and integrated within communities.

blocks.orig: For instance, many blame the Tanzanian government for the ongoing extinction of indigenous languages. Political actions like the wide scale promotion of Swahili and banning ethnic dialects and languages from schools or television make preserving these sub-languages mighty difficult.
blocks.html: Many people, for example, hold the Tanzanian government responsible for the continuing extinction of indigenous languages. Policies such as promoting Swahili on a wide scale and banning ethnic languages and dialects from television or schools make it very hard to preserve these sub-languages.

blocks.orig: For now, though, we can still enjoy and explore the diversity of the Tanzanian linguistic landscape. For how long, we cannot tell…
blocks.html: For the time being, however, the variety of Tanzania’s linguistic landscape is still there for us to enjoy and explore. How long that will last, we cannot say…

blocks.orig: Other languages in Tanzania worth mentioning
blocks.html: Other languages in Tanzania that deserve a mention

blocks.orig: Some languages we don’t want to sweep under the table, are the ‘imported’ ones, such as French, German, Portuguese, Gujarati, Arabic, and Hindustani.
blocks.html: We also don’t want to overlook the ‘imported’ languages, such as French, German, Portuguese, Gujarati, Arabic and Hindustani.

blocks.orig: French, for instance, is another widely spoken languages in Tanzania. It has recently even become part of the school curriculum, and an estimated 1.5 million people in Tanzania are proficient speakers.
blocks.html: French, for example, is one more language widely spoken in Tanzania. It has lately even been added to the school curriculum, and around 1.5 million people in Tanzania are thought to speak it well.

blocks.orig: If we look at the tourism industry, almost all tour operators work with guides speaking English and sometimes even Spanish, French, Italian, German, and Japanese.
blocks.html: In the tourism industry, nearly every tour operator works with English-speaking guides, and sometimes with guides who speak Spanish, French, Italian, German and Japanese too.

blocks.orig: But if you want an authentic Tanzanian experience and communicate in less populated areas, you might want to adopt some Swahili.
blocks.html: Still, if you are after an authentic Tanzanian experience and want to communicate in quieter areas, picking up some Swahili is a good idea.

blocks.orig: Learning some Swahili basics can help you bridge the gap between cultures and make your Tanzania experience much easier – plus you’ll make a lot of people smile, including yourself. So grab a pen, your vocabulary book, and jot down some of these must-knows.
blocks.html: A few basic Swahili words help you bridge cultures and make your Tanzania experience a lot easier – and you will put a smile on many faces, your own included. So take a pen and your vocabulary book, and write down a few of these essentials.

blocks.orig: Hello – Harabi or Mambo (which is more like “What’s up” or “How are things”), and for people older than yourself, you can use Shikamoo, which you can respond with Marhaba
blocks.html: Hello – Harabi or Mambo (closer to “What’s up” or “How are things”), and with people older than you, use Shikamoo, to which the reply is Marhaba

blocks.orig: Goodbye – Kwaheri or kwa herini if referring to more than one person
blocks.html: Goodbye – Kwaheri, or kwa herini when speaking to more than one person

blocks.orig: Nice to meet you – Nafurahi kukuona or Ninafuraha kukutana na wewe
blocks.html: Pleased to meet you – Nafurahi kukuona or Ninafuraha kukutana na wewe

blocks.orig: See you later – Baadaye and Kwa heri for a goodbye over a longer period of time, or Kesho if it’s in the evening, and you won’t see them until the next day
blocks.html: See you later – Baadaye and Kwa heri when you will be apart for longer, or Kesho in the evening when you will not meet again until the following day

blocks.orig: All is good, or I am well – Poa as a response to Mambo, Nzuri as a response to Habari, or Marhaba if the respondent is an older person
blocks.html: Everything is fine, or I am well – Poa in reply to Mambo, Nzuri in reply to Habari, or Marhaba when the person answering is older

blocks.orig: Please – Tafadhali or Naomba if you want to request something politely
blocks.html: Please – Tafadhali, or Naomba to ask for something politely

blocks.orig: Excuse me – Samahani or Pole which also means sorry and shows empathy
blocks.html: Excuse me – Samahani, or Pole, which also means sorry and expresses empathy

blocks.orig: Can you help me? – Tafadhali or naomba msaada
blocks.html: Could you help me? – Tafadhali or naomba msaada

blocks.orig: How do you say (insert word) in Swahili? – Unasemaje (insert word) Kwa Kiswahili
blocks.html: What is (insert word) in Swahili? – Unasemaje (insert word) Kwa Kiswahili

blocks.orig: Where is the (insert place)? – (insert place) iko wapi?
blocks.html: Where can I find the (insert place)? – (insert place) iko wapi?

blocks.orig: Bus station – Stesheni ya basi or Kituo cha mabasi
blocks.html: Bus station – Stesheni ya basi or Kituo cha mabasi

blocks.orig: Where can I find a (insert service)? – (insert service) iko wapi?
blocks.html: Where is there a (insert service)? – (insert service) iko wapi?

blocks.orig: It hurts here  – Inauma hapa or naumwa hapa
blocks.html: I have pain here – Inauma hapa or naumwa hapa

blocks.orig: Of course, you don’t need to get fluent in Tanzania’s national language Swahili before your holiday. As we’ve said, you can definitely manage to navigate this country with English. But if you want to prepare a little in order not to find yourself in a linguistic pickle, we have three tips for you:
blocks.html: You certainly don’t have to become fluent in Swahili, Tanzania’s national language, before your holiday. As mentioned, English will get you around this country without trouble. If you would like to prepare a bit so you don’t end up in a linguistic pickle, though, here are three tips:

blocks.orig: Note down the most important Swahili phrases in a little black book (or red, or brown…) or save them on your phone
blocks.html: Write the key Swahili phrases down in a little black book (or a red one, or brown…) or store them on your phone

blocks.orig: If nothing works, simply ask your guide and smile 🙂
blocks.html: And if all else fails, just ask your guide and smile 🙂

blocks.orig: And should you want to prepare a little more, check out our extensive guide to planning a trip to Tanzania, watch documentaries or read books about Tanzania and by Tanzanians. This way, you are more aware of customs and traditions, making your experience even more authentic. Some typical customs in the country? Greet people, eat food with your right hand, ask permission before taking pictures of people, and respect older people’s views and beliefs.
blocks.html: If you would like to prepare a bit further, have a look at our detailed guide to planning a trip to Tanzania, watch some documentaries or pick up books about Tanzania and by Tanzanians. That way you will know more about local customs and traditions, which makes your experience all the more authentic. A few typical customs here? Greet people, use your right hand to eat, ask before you photograph anyone, and respect the views and beliefs of older people.
